recipes.name: Ghormeh sabzi (herb, lamb and kidney bean stew)
recipes.description: Iran's best-loved stew: lamb simmered slowly with a mountain of fried parsley, coriander, chives and fenugreek, kidney beans and dried limes until dark green, sour and deeply savoury.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans
ingredients.prep: soaked overnight in plenty of cold water

ingredients.name: Dried limes (limoo amani, about 4)
ingredients.prep: rinsed and pierced twice with a knife

ingredients.name: Flat-leaf parsley (about 4 bunches)
ingredients.prep: leaves and tender stems, very finely chopped

ingredients.name: Chives, or the green tops of leeks or spring onions
Dried fenugreek leaves (about 3 tbsp)
ingredients.prep: or 40 g fresh fenugreek leaves, chopped

steps.t: Drain the soaked kidney beans, put them in the saucepan with fresh water to cover by 5 cm and boil hard for 10 minutes; red kidney beans must boil vigorously to destroy their natural toxins. Lower the heat and simmer for 30 minutes, until they are starting to soften, then drain.

Wash the herbs and dry them very thoroughly in a salad spinner and then a tea towel. Chop them very finely by hand, or pulse in a food processor in small batches until finely chopped but not a wet paste.

Heat 4 tablespoons of oil in the large frying pan over medium heat. Add the chopped parsley, coriander and chives and fry, stirring every minute or so, for 20–25 minutes, until they have shrunk to less than half their volume, turned a very dark green and smell toasty. Stir in the dried fenugreek for the last 3 minutes only: it turns bitter if it scorches.

Meanwhile, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the heavy pot over medium-high heat and cook the onions, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes, until golden. Stir in the turmeric for 30 seconds, then add the lamb and brown it on all sides for 8–10 minutes.
Pour in the water, add the drained beans, salt and pepper and bring to the boil. Skim off any grey foam, then cover, lower the heat and simmer gently for 1 hour.

Stir in the fried herbs and the pierced dried limes. Cover again and simmer on low heat for 1½–2 hours, stirring now and then and adding a splash of hot water if it gets too thick. It is ready when the lamb is very tender, the beans are creamy and a dark green film of oil rises to the surface.

Taste the stew: it should be sour, herby and savoury. Press the limes against the side of the pot to release more sourness, add lemon juice if it needs more tang, and adjust the salt. Lift the limes out if you prefer the stew less bitter. Rest it off the heat for 10 minutes.
Serve with chelow (steamed saffron rice) and its crisp tahdig, with yogurt, radishes and fresh herbs alongside. Like most khoresh, ghormeh sabzi tastes even better the next day.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months; the flavour deepens overnight.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Beef chuck works the same way. With canned kidney beans (1 can, drained), skip the first step and add them for the last 30 minutes.
Ready-fried frozen ghormeh sabzi herbs from Persian grocers save the long herb-frying step; use about 400 g.

recipes.name: Fesenjan (chicken in walnut and pomegranate sauce)
recipes.description: Chicken simmered in a thick, glossy sauce of slow-cooked ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses, balanced sweet and sour. A festive stew served with saffron rice.

ingredients.name: Sugar
ingredients.prep: more or less, to balance the sourness

steps.t: Toast the walnuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan, until they smell nutty and are a shade darker. Cool for 5 minutes, then grind in the food processor to a fine, damp meal that is just starting to clump; stop before it turns into butter.

Put the ground walnuts and water in the heavy pot and bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat. Cook, partly covered, for 1 hour, stirring from the bottom every 10 minutes because it catches easily. The sauce is ready for the next stage when it has darkened to a light coffee colour and beads of walnut oil appear on the surface.

Meanwhile, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion for 8–10 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the turmeric, then push the onion to one side, season the chicken with the salt and pepper and brown it lightly for 3–4 minutes per side.

Stir the pomegranate molasses, sugar and cinnamon into the walnut sauce and taste it: it should be clearly sour with a rounded sweetness behind it. Add more molasses for tang or a little more sugar if it is sharp, remembering it will concentrate as it cooks.

Add the chicken and onions to the sauce, cover and simmer on low heat for 40–45 minutes, stirring now and then and adding a splash of hot water if it gets too thick. It is done when the chicken is tender and reaches 74 °C, and the sauce is thick, glossy and a deep chocolate brown with a sheen of oil.
Rest the stew off the heat for 10 minutes and adjust the salt. Scatter with pomegranate seeds and serve with chelow (steamed saffron rice) and a simple herb or cucumber salad to cut the richness.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring, until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F); the sauce thickens in the fridge.
notes: Duck legs or meatballs of minced lamb are traditional alternatives to chicken; brands of pomegranate molasses vary a lot in sourness, so always taste.

recipes.name: Joojeh kabab (saffron chicken kebab)
recipes.description: Chicken marinated in grated onion, lemon, yogurt and saffron, then grilled on skewers and basted with saffron butter. Served with rice, grilled tomatoes and sumac.

ingredients.name: Chicken thighs or breast, boneless and skinless
Saffron threads
ingredients.prep: ground with a pinch of sugar and steeped in 3 tbsp hot water

steps.t: Grind the saffron threads with a pinch of sugar in the mortar to a fine powder, then pour over 3 tablespoons of hot (not boiling) water and leave to steep for 10 minutes, until deep orange-red.

Grate the onion on the fine side of a box grater into the mixing bowl, keeping all the juice. Stir in the yogurt, lemon juice, olive oil, salt, pepper and two-thirds of the saffron water. Add the chicken and massage the marinade in well. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, but no longer than 24 hours or the acid makes the meat mushy.

Light the charcoal and let it burn down to glowing coals with a coat of white ash, or heat the oven grill to high. Thread the chicken onto the flat skewers with the pieces touching but not packed, scraping off clinging bits of onion, which burn. Thread the tomatoes onto a separate skewer.
Melt the butter with the remaining saffron water and a squeeze of lemon juice to make the basting butter.

Grill the chicken 8–10 cm above the coals for 10–12 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes and brushing with the saffron butter, until golden with charred edges and the thickest piece reaches 74 °C with clear juices. Grill the tomatoes alongside until blistered and soft, 6–8 minutes. Under an oven grill, allow 14–16 minutes, turning once.

Slide the chicken off the skewers onto a warm platter (a sheet of flatbread underneath soaks up the juices), brush with the rest of the butter and rest for 3 minutes. Serve with chelow rice, the grilled tomatoes, lemon wedges and a sprinkle of sumac.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Traditionally made with bone-in pieces of young chicken; bone-in thighs need 18–20 minutes on the grill.

recipes.name: Kabab koobideh (minced lamb and beef kebab)
recipes.description: Long, juicy kebabs of minced lamb and beef with grated onion, kneaded until sticky and grilled on wide skewers. With saffron rice it becomes chelow kabab, Iran's national dish.

ingredients.name: Butter
ingredients.prep: melted with a pinch of bloomed saffron, for brushing

steps.t: Grate the onion finely, tip it into the tea towel and squeeze hard over the sink until no more juice comes out. This matters: a wet mixture slides off the skewers. Discard the juice.

Put both meats in a large bowl with the squeezed onion, salt, pepper and turmeric. Knead firmly with one hand for 5 minutes, squeezing the mixture through your fingers, until it turns paler, sticky and paste-like, and stretches rather than breaks when you pull a piece apart. Cover and chill for at least 30 minutes (up to overnight) so the fat firms.

Light the charcoal and let it burn to glowing embers, or heat the oven grill to its highest setting. Divide the meat into 8 portions. With wet hands, squeeze a portion around a skewer, then work it along the skewer into a flat kebab about 1.5 cm thick and 20 cm long, pinching it at intervals to leave finger-ridges. Press the ends firmly onto the metal.

Lay the skewers over the coals, resting their ends on the sides of the grill so the meat does not touch the grate. Turn them constantly for the first minute so the meat sets evenly and does not drop, then grill for 6–8 minutes in total, turning every couple of minutes, until browned, juicy and cooked through to 71 °C. Grill the tomatoes alongside, cut side down first.
Brush the kebabs with the saffron butter and slide them off the skewers onto warm plates with a piece of flatbread to grip them.
Serve straight away over chelow rice topped with a knob of butter, with the grilled tomatoes, raw onion slices and sumac sprinkled over the meat at the table.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: No grill? Shape the mixture into long flat kebabs on a lined tray and cook under a very hot oven grill for 10–12 minutes, turning once.

recipes.name: Zereshk polo ba morgh (barberry rice with saffron chicken)
recipes.description: Fluffy steamed basmati crowned with saffron rice, buttery sweet-sour barberries and pistachios, served with chicken braised in onion, saffron and tomato. A wedding and party favourite.
equipment: Non-stick pot with a lid (24 cm)

ingredients.name: Chicken legs or thighs, bone-in and skinless
Basmati rice
ingredients.prep: rinsed until clear and soaked for 1–2 hours

ingredients.name: Saffron threads
ingredients.prep: ground and steeped in 4 tbsp hot water

ingredients.name: Dried barberries (zereshk)
ingredients.prep: picked over for stems and grit

steps.t: For the chicken, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the turmeric, then add the chicken and brown it for 3–4 minutes per side. Stir in the tomato paste, half the saffron water, the salt, pepper and water. Cover and simmer on low heat for 45–50 minutes, turning once, until the chicken is tender, reaches 74 °C near the bone and the sauce has reduced to a thick glaze.

Meanwhile, bring 3 litres of water and the 2 tablespoons of salt to a rolling boil in the large pot. Drain the soaked rice, add it and boil uncovered for 6–8 minutes, stirring gently once, until the grains have lengthened and are soft outside but a grain snapped in half still shows a small white core. Drain in the fine colander and rinse briefly with lukewarm water.

Heat 3 tablespoons of oil with 2 tablespoons of water in the non-stick pot. Scatter in a thin layer of rice and press it down firmly for the tahdig crust, then spoon in the rest loosely, building a pyramid. Poke 5 holes to the bottom with the handle of a wooden spoon and dot the butter over the top.

Wrap the lid in the tea towel, tying the corners over the handle so they cannot reach the flame, and cover the pot tightly. Cook over medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes, until you hear a steady sizzle and see steam, then turn the heat to the lowest setting and steam for 45–50 minutes. The rice should be fluffy and every grain separate.

While the rice steams, soak the barberries in cold water for 10 minutes, then lift them out, leaving any grit behind. Melt the butter in a small pan over low heat, add the barberries and sugar and stir for 1–2 minutes, only until they plump and turn glossy; they burn and turn bitter very quickly.

Mix a large spoonful of the steamed rice with the remaining saffron water to make golden rice. Spoon the white rice onto a platter, cover it with the saffron rice, then scatter over the barberries and pistachios. Lift out the tahdig in pieces and arrange it around the edge.
Serve the chicken and its sauce alongside, with plain yogurt and a herb salad. Spoon a little of the sauce over the rice on each plate.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Dried barberries are sold in Persian and Middle Eastern shops; dried sour cherries or unsweetened cranberries, chopped, are the closest stand-ins.

recipes.name: Chelow ba tahdig (Persian steamed rice with a crisp crust)
recipes.description: Parboiled basmati steamed slowly until every grain is long and separate, with a golden saffron-yogurt crust (tahdig) on the bottom of the pot. The rice under every Persian stew and kebab.
equipment: Non-stick pot with a lid (24 cm)

ingredients.name: Basmati rice
ingredients.prep: rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.name: Saffron threads
ingredients.prep: ground and steeped in 4 tbsp hot water

steps.t: Rinse the rice gently in several changes of cold water, swirling with your fingers, until the water runs clear. Cover with fresh cold water, stir in 1 tablespoon of the salt and soak for 1–2 hours; long-soaked rice cooks into longer, more separate grains.

Bring 3 litres of water with the remaining salt to a rolling boil in the large pot. Drain the rice, add it and boil uncovered for 5–7 minutes, stirring gently once, until the grains are long and bend easily but still have a tiny hard core when bitten. Drain in the fine colander and rinse with lukewarm water to stop the cooking.

In a bowl, mix about 1 cup of the parboiled rice with the yogurt, 1 tablespoon of the saffron water and 1 tablespoon of oil. Heat the remaining oil with the 2 tablespoons of water in the non-stick pot over medium heat, spread the yogurt rice over the base and press it down firmly with the back of a spoon.

Spoon the rest of the rice on top loosely, heaping it into a pyramid away from the sides; don't press it. Make 4–5 holes down to the base with the handle of a wooden spoon so steam can escape, and dot the butter over the top.

Wrap the lid in the tea towel, tie the corners up over the handle, and cover the pot tightly. Cook over medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes, until steam escapes and you hear a steady sizzle, then reduce to the lowest heat and steam for 50–55 minutes without lifting the lid.

Drizzle the remaining saffron water over one side of the rice and spoon the rice onto a platter, mixing the golden and white grains lightly. Set the pot base in a sink with 2 cm of cold water for 1 minute to loosen the crust, then turn it out whole onto a plate or lift it out in pieces. It should be golden and shatteringly crisp.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with water and reheat covered until steaming hot throughout; the tahdig is best eaten fresh.
notes: For potato tahdig, line the oiled base with 5 mm slices of peeled potato instead of the yogurt rice.

recipes.name: Kuku sabzi (Persian herb frittata)
recipes.description: A thick, emerald-green frittata that is mostly herbs bound with egg, studded with walnuts and barberries. Made for Nowruz and eaten warm or cold with yogurt and flatbread.
equipment: Non-stick frying pan with a lid (24 cm)

steps.t: Wash the herbs and dry them very well, first in the salad spinner and then rolled in a tea towel; wet herbs make a soggy kuku that won't set. Chop them finely with a sharp knife.

In the large bowl, whisk the eggs with the flour, baking powder, turmeric, salt and pepper until no lumps of flour remain. Fold in the chopped herbs, fenugreek, walnuts and barberries. The mixture should look like herbs barely held together by egg, more green than yellow.

Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat until it shimmers. Pour in the mixture and level it with a spatula. Cover, turn the heat to low and cook for 15–18 minutes, until the edges are set and the top is mostly firm; the underside should be a deep green-brown, not black.

To turn it, slide the kuku onto a large plate, put the pan upside down over it and flip both together (or cut it into quarters in the pan and turn each with a spatula). Pour the remaining oil around the edge, cover and cook for 8–10 minutes more, until firm when pressed in the centre with no liquid egg.
Slide it onto a board and leave to settle for 5 minutes, then cut into wedges or diamonds. It can also be baked in an oiled 20 cm dish at 180 °C for 30–35 minutes.
Serve warm or at room temperature with yogurt, flatbread, radishes, walnuts and feta, or tucked into bread as a sandwich for a picnic.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Eat cold or at room temperature, or warm in a low oven for 10 minutes.
notes: Some families add a finely chopped leek or a little spinach; keep the total weight of greens about the same.

recipes.name: Ash reshteh (Persian noodle, bean and herb soup)
recipes.description: A thick, hearty soup of beans, lentils, herbs and spinach with tangy kashk and Persian noodles, topped with fried onions, garlic and sizzling mint oil. Made for Nowruz and cold days.

ingredients.name: Kashk, or thick strained yogurt thinned with a little water

steps.t: Drain the soaked kidney beans and chickpeas and put them in the large pot with the water. Boil hard for 10 minutes, skimming off the foam (kidney beans must boil vigorously), then simmer for 40 minutes. Add the lentils and simmer for 20 minutes more, until the beans are nearly tender.

Meanwhile, heat 5 tablespoons of oil in the wide frying pan over medium heat. Fry the onions, stirring often and more frequently as they darken, for 20–25 minutes, until deep golden brown and sweet. Stir the turmeric into half the onions and add them to the pot; keep the rest for the topping.

Add the parsley, coriander, dill, spinach and spring onions to the pot with the salt and pepper. Simmer for 30 minutes, stirring often from the bottom, until the greens have collapsed, the beans are creamy and the soup is thick and dark green. Add hot water if it gets too stiff to stir.
Add the noodles and simmer for 10–12 minutes, stirring so they don't stick to the base, until tender. The starch thickens the soup further; it should be thick but still spoonable.

For the garlic chips, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the small pan over low heat and fry the garlic for 1–2 minutes, until pale gold; lift it out. Add the last tablespoon of oil, take the pan off the heat and stir in the dried mint for 10–20 seconds, until it darkens and smells fragrant. Burnt mint is bitter, so work quickly.
Loosen the kashk or strained yogurt with a few spoonfuls of water and stir about half of it into the pot off the heat. Taste and adjust the salt.
Ladle into bowls and top each with a swirl of the remaining kashk, the fried onions, garlic chips and a drizzle of mint oil. Serve hot with flatbread.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; keep the toppings separately. The noodles soften and the soup thickens as it stands.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with hot water and reheat until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F).
notes: Kashk (fermented whey) is sold in jars at Persian grocers and is saltier and tangier than yogurt; season after adding it.

recipes.name: Sholeh zard (saffron rice pudding)
recipes.description: A golden, dairy-free rice pudding perfumed with saffron, rose water and cardamom, decorated with cinnamon and pistachios. Made in large pots to share at religious holidays and Nowruz.

ingredients.name: Basmati or other long-grain rice
ingredients.prep: rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.name: Saffron threads
ingredients.prep: ground and steeped in 3 tbsp hot water

steps.t: Rinse the rice several times until the water runs clear, then put it in the heavy saucepan with the water. Bring to the boil, skim off the starchy foam, then simmer uncovered over medium-low heat for 25–30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the grains are swollen, splitting and the mixture looks like thin porridge.
Add the sugar a third at a time, stirring until each addition dissolves. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring frequently and scraping the bottom, because the sugar makes it catch.

Stir in the saffron water, oil, almonds and cardamom. Cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes more, stirring often, until the pudding coats the spoon thickly and falls from it in a slow ribbon. It firms a lot as it cools, so don't cook it until stiff.
Stir in the rose water for the last 5 minutes so its fragrance stays fresh, then turn off the heat, cover and leave to rest for 5 minutes.

Pour into shallow dishes and smooth the tops. Leave to cool until a skin forms, about 30 minutes, then decorate with fine lines of cinnamon (traditional patterns are lattices or names) and the pistachios.
Serve at room temperature or chilled, in small portions: it is very sweet and rich in perfume.

recipes.storage: Cover and refrigerate for up to 4 days.
notes: Butter instead of oil is common and gives a richer pudding; oil keeps it dairy-free.

recipes.name: Çılbır (poached eggs on garlic yogurt)
recipes.description: Softly poached eggs on cool garlicky strained yogurt, drenched in sizzling butter with Aleppo-style chilli flakes. An Ottoman palace dish that is now a Turkish breakfast favourite.

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.prep: grated or crushed to a paste

ingredients.name: Crusty bread or simit, to serve

steps.t: Take the yogurt out of the fridge early: cold yogurt chills the eggs. Mix it with the garlic and a pinch of the salt and spread it into two shallow bowls.
Bring about 8 cm of water to a bare simmer in the wide saucepan over medium heat and add the vinegar; the surface should just tremble, with small bubbles at the base.

Crack an egg into the small cup; very fresh eggs hold together best. Stir the water to make a gentle whirlpool and slide the egg into the centre, where the swirl wraps the white around the yolk. Add a second egg the same way at the side of the pan.

Poach for 3–4 minutes, until the whites are firm and opaque but the yolks still feel soft when nudged with the slotted spoon. Lift the eggs out onto kitchen paper to drain, trim any ragged white with scissors, and poach the other two.

Meanwhile, melt the butter in the small frying pan over medium heat and let it foam for about 2 minutes, until it smells nutty and flecks of milk solids turn light brown. Take it off the heat and stir in the pul biber and paprika: they should sizzle and turn the butter brick red.
Set two eggs on each bowl of yogurt, spoon the hot chilli butter over the top and sprinkle with the remaining salt and the dill. Serve immediately with bread for dipping into the yolk and yogurt.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately.

recipes.name: Adana kebab (spiced minced lamb kebab)
recipes.description: Hand-minced fatty lamb kneaded with red pepper and chilli flakes, pressed onto wide skewers and grilled over charcoal. Served on flatbread with sumac onions and blistered tomatoes and peppers.

ingredients.name: Red bell pepper (or Turkish kapya pepper)
ingredients.prep: very finely chopped and squeezed dry

ingredients.name: Pul biber (chilli flakes), or to taste

steps.t: Wrap the chopped red pepper in the tea towel and squeeze out as much juice as you can; excess moisture makes the meat fall off the skewers.

Put the lamb, pepper, pul biber, paprika and salt in the bowl and knead firmly for 5–8 minutes, until the mixture is sticky, slightly paler and holds together in one mass when you lift it. Cover and chill for 30 minutes to firm the fat.

Light the charcoal and let it burn down to glowing coals, or heat the oven grill to high. Divide the meat into 8 portions. With wet hands, mould each onto a skewer into a flattish kebab about 2 cm thick and 20 cm long, pinching along its length to make shallow ridges and sealing the ends tightly against the metal.
For the sumac onions, rub the sliced onion with a pinch of salt for 30 seconds, rinse, squeeze dry and toss with the sumac and parsley.

Grill the kebabs over the hot coals, turning every minute or so, for 8–10 minutes, until well browned and sizzling and cooked through to 71 °C. Grill the tomatoes and green peppers alongside until blistered and soft.

Warm the flatbreads over the grill and press them onto the kebabs to soak up the juices as you slide the meat off the skewers. Serve the kebabs on the bread with the sumac onions, grilled tomatoes and peppers, and a glass of ayran.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In Adana the lamb is chopped by hand with a wide blade (zırh) together with tail fat; asking your butcher for coarsely minced lamb shoulder with its fat comes close.

recipes.name: İmam bayıldı (olive-oil braised stuffed aubergines)
recipes.description: Whole aubergines fried until silky, split and filled with slow-cooked onion, garlic and tomato, then baked in olive oil. A classic zeytinyağlı dish served at room temperature.

steps.t: Peel the aubergines in lengthways stripes to give a zebra pattern, leaving the stalks on. Soak them for 20 minutes in a bowl of water with the 1½ tablespoons of salt to draw out bitterness, then drain and pat completely dry.

Heat 5 tablespoons of the oil in the wide frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the aubergines, turning every couple of minutes, for 10–12 minutes, until golden all over and soft enough to collapse when pressed. Drain on kitchen paper.

Lower the heat to medium, add 3 tablespoons of oil to the pan and cook the onions with a pinch of salt for 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until very soft, sweet and pale gold; don't let them brown. Add the garlic and chopped green pepper for 2 minutes, then the chopped tomatoes, tomato paste, sugar and salt and cook for 5 minutes, until thick and jammy. Stir in the parsley.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Lay the aubergines in the baking dish and slit each one lengthways down the middle, stopping 1 cm from each end, then press the flesh apart to make a deep pocket. Spoon in the filling generously and top each with a slice of tomato and strips of green pepper.

Mix the hot water with the remaining oil and pour it around (not over) the aubergines. Cover with foil and bake for 35 minutes, then uncover and bake for 10 minutes more, until the aubergines are meltingly tender and most of the liquid has reduced to a glossy juice.
Leave to cool in the dish to room temperature, at least 1 hour, spooning the juices over now and then; like all zeytinyağlı dishes it tastes best cool, when the flavours have settled.
Serve one or two aubergines per person with crusty bread to mop up the oil, and yogurt or cacık alongside if you like.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in the dish, covered, for up to 4 days; bring back to room temperature before serving.
notes: The name means 'the imam fainted', supposedly at the amount of olive oil; don't skimp on it, as it carries the flavour.

recipes.name: Lahmacun (thin flatbread with spiced minced meat)
recipes.description: Paper-thin yeasted flatbreads spread with minced lamb, peppers, tomato and herbs, baked very hot until crisp at the edges. Rolled up with parsley, sumac onions and lemon.
equipment: Baking steel, stone or heavy baking tray

ingredients.name: Minced lamb (or half lamb, half beef)
Long green pepper or green chilli
Red pepper paste (biber salçası), or more tomato paste
Small red onion
ingredients.prep: thinly sliced and tossed with 1 tsp sumac

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl, add the water and oil and bring together into a dough. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic and it springs back slowly when pressed. Cover and leave to rise in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.

For the topping, chop the onion, peppers, tomatoes, garlic and parsley very finely by hand, or pulse them in a food processor until finely minced but not puréed. Tip into a sieve and press out the excess juice, then mix with the lamb, both pastes, the spices, salt and pepper, kneading until it becomes a soft, spreadable paste.
Put the baking steel or heavy tray on the top shelf and heat the oven to its highest setting (250 °C or more) for at least 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and rest them under a cloth for 10 minutes. Roll each out on a floured surface into a very thin oval, about 2 mm thick and 25 cm long.

Spread about 3 tablespoons of topping over each base with your fingertips, taking it right to the edges and pressing it into the dough in a thin, even layer; a thick layer stays raw and makes the bread soggy.

Slide two lahmacun at a time onto the hot steel and bake for 6–8 minutes, until the edges are crisp and browned, the base is spotted underneath and the meat is cooked through with no pink. Stack the baked breads under a clean tea towel so they stay soft enough to roll.
To eat, squeeze lemon over a lahmacun, scatter with parsley and sumac onions, roll it up tightly and eat with your hands, with ayran alongside.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot oven or dry frying pan for 2–3 minutes until hot throughout.

recipes.name: Cacık (yogurt with cucumber, garlic and mint)
recipes.description: Cool, loose yogurt with grated cucumber, garlic and dried mint, thinned with cold water so it can be eaten with a spoon. Served alongside kebabs, pilaf and köfte, or as a chilled summer soup.

ingredients.name: Cucumbers
ingredients.prep: peeled in stripes and finely diced or grated

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.prep: crushed with a pinch of salt

steps.t: Dice or coarsely grate the cucumber, sprinkle with a pinch of the salt and leave for 5 minutes. Squeeze it lightly; cacık is meant to be loose, so you don't need to wring it dry.
Crush the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt using the flat of a knife.
Whisk the yogurt in the bowl until smooth, then stir in the garlic, cucumber and the dill if using. Rub the dried mint between your palms over the bowl to release its aroma and stir most of it in.

Whisk in the cold water a little at a time until the cacık is the consistency of thick soup; use less water for a dip. Taste for salt, then chill for 10 minutes. Serve drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with the rest of the mint, with an ice cube in each bowl on hot days.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 2 days; stir before serving.

recipes.name: Kısır (spiced bulgur salad)
recipes.description: Fine bulgur soaked and kneaded with tomato and pepper pastes, then tossed with herbs, spring onions, pomegranate molasses and lemon. Tangy, gently spicy and a fixture of Turkish tea gatherings.

ingredients.name: Red pepper paste (biber salçası), mild or hot

steps.t: Put the bulgur in the large bowl, pour over the boiling water, stir once and cover with a plate. Leave for 10–15 minutes, until the water is absorbed and the grains are tender with a slight bite.

While the bulgur is still warm, add both pastes, the oil, pul biber, cumin and salt. Knead with your hands (gloves help) for 2–3 minutes, until every grain is evenly coated and red; the warmth helps it take up the flavours.
Add the spring onions, parsley, mint, tomatoes and cucumber with the pomegranate molasses and lemon juice and toss gently until evenly mixed.

Taste: it should be tangy, slightly sweet and gently spicy, so adjust with more lemon, molasses, salt or pul biber. Leave for 10 minutes for the flavours to settle, then pile into a dish and serve with lettuce leaves for scooping, and lemon wedges.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 3 days; add the cucumber just before serving if making ahead.

recipes.name: Fıstıklı baklava (pistachio baklava)
recipes.description: Dozens of paper-thin layers of filo brushed with clarified butter around a thick layer of ground pistachios, baked until crisp and soaked in lemon syrup. Gaziantep's pride and an Eid essential.

ingredients.name: Filo pastry (about 24 sheets)
ingredients.prep: thawed in the fridge if frozen

ingredients.name: Shelled unsalted pistachios
ingredients.prep: finely ground, 2 tbsp kept for garnish

steps.t: Make the syrup first so it has time to cool completely. Bring the sugar and water to the boil in the medium saucepan, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then simmer for 10 minutes without stirring. Add the lemon juice, simmer 1 minute more and leave to cool.

Clarify the butter: melt it in the small saucepan over low heat for 8–10 minutes, skim off the white foam, then carefully pour the clear golden fat into a jug, leaving the milky solids behind. Clarified butter makes the layers crisper and won't burn.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Brush the tin with butter. Trim the filo to fit the tin if needed and keep the stack covered with a barely damp tea towel while you work, as it dries out and cracks within minutes.

Lay in a sheet of filo and brush it lightly but completely with butter. Repeat with 11 more sheets, buttering each. Spread the ground pistachios evenly over the pastry, then cover with the remaining sheets one at a time, brushing each with butter. Brush the top sheet generously.

With a very sharp knife, cut the baklava all the way through into diamonds or 4 cm squares before baking; it cannot be cut cleanly once baked. Pour the remaining butter evenly over the top so it runs into the cuts.
Bake for 45–50 minutes, until deep golden all over, crisp and the layers have puffed and separated. If the top browns too fast, lower the oven to 160 °C for the last 15 minutes.
Take the tin out and immediately ladle the cooled syrup slowly and evenly over the hot baklava; it should sizzle loudly. Hot pastry with cool syrup keeps the layers crisp.

Leave uncovered at room temperature for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, to absorb the syrup. Sprinkle with the reserved pistachios, recut along the lines and serve in small pieces with Turkish tea or coffee.

recipes.storage: Keep at room temperature, loosely covered, for up to 5 days; refrigerating softens the pastry.
notes: Walnuts (cevizli baklava) are the everyday alternative to pistachios.

recipes.name: Ayran (salted yogurt drink)
recipes.description: Yogurt whisked with cold water and a little salt into a frothy, refreshing drink. Turkey's national drink, served with kebabs, lahmacun and pide.

steps.t: Put the yogurt in the jug and whisk until completely smooth, with no lumps left; any lumps stay in the finished drink.
Pour in the cold water gradually, whisking hard, or blend everything in a blender for 30 seconds. About equal parts yogurt and water is classic; use less water for a thicker drink.
Add the salt and whisk until the ayran is foamy on top. Taste: it should be tangy and lightly salty, never sweet.
Pour into glasses with a good head of froth, over ice if you like, and serve straight away with grilled meat, lahmacun or pide. Garnish with a mint leaf.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; it separates on standing, so whisk again before serving. Keeps 1 day refrigerated.

recipes.name: Ezogelin çorbası (red lentil, bulgur and mint soup)
recipes.description: A thick, unblended soup of red lentils, bulgur and a little rice in a pepper-paste broth, finished with sizzling dried mint and chilli. Named after a legendary bride from Gaziantep.

ingredients.name: Red pepper paste (biber salçası), or more tomato paste

steps.t: Put the lentils, bulgur and rice in the sieve and rinse under cold running water until the water runs almost clear.

Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat and cook the onion for 5 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then both pastes and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes, until they darken and smell sweet.

Add the rinsed lentils, bulgur and rice and the water. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then partly cover and simmer for 30–35 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils have dissolved and the bulgur and rice are tender. Ezogelin is not blended: it should be thick and slightly textured.
Season with the cumin, half the mint and the salt. If it is thicker than you like, loosen it with hot water; it thickens further as it stands.

Just before serving, heat the olive oil (or butter) in the small pan over medium heat, add the remaining mint and the pul biber and let them sizzle for 10–15 seconds, until fragrant, then take the pan off the heat.
Ladle the soup into bowls, drizzle each with the red mint oil and serve with lemon wedges to squeeze in and fresh bread.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F).

recipes.name: Tolma (Armenian vine leaves stuffed with lamb and rice)
recipes.description: Tender vine leaves wrapped around minced lamb and beef, rice and plenty of herbs, simmered gently and served warm with garlicky yogurt. A staple of Armenian family tables.
equipment: Wide heavy pot with a lid
Heatproof plate that fits inside the pot

steps.t: Unroll the vine leaves, rinse them well and blanch in a saucepan of boiling water for 2 minutes to soften them and wash away the brine. Drain, snip off any stems and set aside any torn leaves for lining the pot.

Put the lamb, beef, rice, onions, herbs, dried mint, paprika, salt and pepper in the bowl with 4 tablespoons of cold water. Knead with your hand for 2–3 minutes, until evenly mixed and slightly sticky.

Lay a leaf shiny side down with the stem end towards you. Put a heaped tablespoon of filling in a short log just above the stem end, fold the bottom over it, fold in both sides and roll up firmly into a neat cylinder about 6 cm long. Don't roll too tightly: the rice swells as it cooks. Repeat with the rest.

Line the base of the pot with the torn leaves. Pack the tolma in snugly, seam side down, in tight layers. Whisk the tomato paste into the hot water, pour it over to just cover, dot with the butter and set the plate on top to keep the rolls from unravelling.

Bring to a gentle simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 60–70 minutes, until the leaves are tender, the rice is soft and most of the liquid has been absorbed. Cut one open to check that the meat is cooked through and steaming (71 °C).
Take off the heat and rest, covered, for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, stir the yogurt with the crushed garlic and salt.
Serve the tolma warm with the garlic yogurt spooned over and lavash or crusty bread for the juices.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a covered pan with a splash of water until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F).
notes: In summer Armenians also make tolma with stuffed peppers, tomatoes and aubergines, and in winter with cabbage leaves (kaghambi tolma).

recipes.name: Zeytinyağlı yaprak sarma (vine leaves stuffed with herbed rice)
recipes.description: Slim vine-leaf rolls filled with rice cooked with onion, pine nuts, currants, allspice and herbs, simmered in olive oil and lemon and eaten cool. The meatless mezze version of dolma.
equipment: Wide heavy pot with a lid
Heatproof plate that fits inside the pot

steps.t: Unroll the vine leaves, rinse them and blanch in a saucepan of boiling water for 2 minutes to soften them and remove the brine. Drain, cut off the stems and keep any torn leaves for lining the pot.

Heat 6 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions with a pinch of salt for 10 minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the pine nuts and stir for 2–3 minutes, until golden, then add the rice and stir for 3 minutes, until the grains turn translucent at the edges.

Stir in the currants, allspice, cinnamon, dried mint, pepper, sugar, salt and the 200 ml of hot water. Cover and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes, until the water is absorbed but the rice is still firm in the centre; it finishes cooking inside the leaves. Off the heat, stir in the dill and parsley and leave until cool enough to handle.

Lay a leaf shiny side down, veins up, with the stem end towards you. Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in a thin log near the stem end, fold the bottom over, fold in the sides and roll up into a slim finger about 7 cm long, firm but not tight. Repeat with the rest.

Line the pot with the torn leaves. Pack the rolls in tightly, seam side down, in layers. Pour over the remaining oil, the lemon juice and enough hot water to just cover, then weigh them down with the heatproof plate.
Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on low heat for 40–45 minutes, until the rice is tender, the leaves are silky and most of the liquid has been absorbed.

Leave to cool completely in the pot, at least 2 hours; they firm up and soak up the oil as they cool. Arrange on a platter and serve at room temperature or lightly chilled with lemon wedges, and yogurt if you like.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 5 days; serve cool or at room temperature.
notes: Fresh young vine leaves in early summer are the best of all: blanch them for 30 seconds.

recipes.name: Fattoush (bread salad with sumac dressing)
recipes.description: Crunchy chopped salad of lettuce, tomato, cucumber, radish and herbs with toasted pita, dressed with lemon, sumac and pomegranate molasses. The bread is added at the last moment so it stays crisp.
equipment: Small bowl or jar for the dressing

ingredients.name: Pita breads, ideally a day old
ingredients.prep: split and torn into bite-sized pieces

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Toss the torn pita with 2 tablespoons of oil, the sumac and a pinch of salt and spread on the baking tray. Bake for 6–8 minutes, shaking the tray once, until golden and crisp right through. Cool on the tray; they crisp further as they cool. (Frying the pieces in hot oil is the richer traditional option.)
For the dressing, whisk the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses, garlic, sumac, dried mint and salt in the small bowl, then whisk in the olive oil until slightly thickened.
Put the lettuce, tomatoes, cucumbers, radishes, pepper, spring onions, parsley and mint in the large bowl. The salad can wait in the fridge at this point for up to an hour.

Just before serving, pour over the dressing and toss well. Add most of the toasted bread and toss once more, then scatter the remaining bread on top, sprinkle with a little more sumac and serve straight away, before the bread softens.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; undressed vegetables keep 1 day refrigerated, and the bread keeps crisp in an airtight tin.
notes: Purslane (baqleh) is a classic addition when you can find it.

recipes.name: Baba ghanoush (smoky aubergine and tahini dip)
recipes.description: Aubergines charred until smoky and collapsing, mashed with tahini, lemon and garlic and finished with olive oil and pomegranate. Also known as mutabbal in much of the Levant.
equipment: Gas hob, barbecue or oven grill

steps.t: Prick the aubergines a few times with a fork. Set them directly on a gas flame, on a hot barbecue or under a very hot oven grill and cook, turning with tongs every few minutes, until the skin is blackened and blistered all over and the aubergines have completely collapsed: 15–20 minutes over a flame, 30–40 minutes under a grill. The charring gives the smoky flavour.

Put them in a bowl, cover with a plate and leave for 10 minutes; the steam loosens the skin. Split them open, scoop the soft flesh into the colander and discard the skin and stalks. Leave to drain for 10 minutes to get rid of the bitter juices.
Crush the garlic with the salt to a paste. Chop the aubergine flesh finely with a knife or mash it with a fork, keeping a little texture, then mix in the garlic, tahini and lemon juice.

Taste: it should be smoky, creamy and bright, so add more lemon or salt if needed. Spread on a plate, make a swirl with the back of a spoon, drizzle with olive oil and scatter with parsley and pomegranate seeds. Serve with warm pita and raw vegetables.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 3 days; add the garnish just before serving.

recipes.name: Kibbeh bil sanieh (baked kibbeh with pine nut filling)
recipes.description: A tray of fine bulgur and lean meat pressed in two layers around spiced lamb, onion and pine nuts, scored into diamonds and baked until crisp. Lebanon's national dish in its easiest form.
equipment: Baking tray or round tin (about 30 cm)

ingredients.name: Very lean minced beef or lamb

steps.t: Rinse the bulgur in the sieve, then cover it with cold water and soak for 15 minutes. Drain and squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands.

For the filling, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and toast the pine nuts for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until golden; lift them out. Add the onions and cook for 8 minutes, until soft and golden, then add the lamb and cook on high heat for 8–10 minutes, breaking it up, until browned with no pink left. Season with the allspice, cinnamon, salt and pepper, stir in the pine nuts and leave to cool.

For the shell, pulse the grated onion with the spices and salt in the food processor. Add the lean meat and the bulgur and process in two batches, adding iced water a spoonful at a time, until it forms a smooth, sticky, dough-like paste that holds together when pressed. Knead the batches together briefly by hand.

Heat the oven to 190 °C and brush the tray with oil. Press half the shell mixture evenly over the base, about 1 cm thick, smoothing it with wet hands. Spread the cooled filling over it in an even layer.

Flatten handfuls of the remaining shell between wet palms into thin patties and lay them over the filling, overlapping slightly, then smooth and press the joins together with wet hands so the top is sealed.

Dip a sharp knife in water and score the top into diamonds, cutting through the top layer only, and run the knife around the edge. Make a small hole in the centre and drizzle the remaining oil all over so it runs into the cuts.
Bake for 35–40 minutes, until deep golden brown and crisp on top and the edges have pulled away from the tray. Rest for 10 minutes, then cut along the scored lines.
Serve warm or at room temperature with yogurt or yogurt and cucumber salad, fattoush or a simple tomato salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Shish tawook (garlic and lemon chicken skewers with toum)
recipes.description: Chicken breast marinated in yogurt, lemon, garlic and paprika, grilled on skewers until charred at the edges and served with fluffy whipped garlic sauce (toum), pickles and pita.

steps.t: Whisk the yogurt, lemon juice, olive oil, crushed garlic, tomato paste, paprika, thyme, salt and pepper in the bowl. Add the chicken, turn to coat and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or up to 12 hours.

Make the toum: blend the garlic and salt in the food processor, scraping down the sides, until finely minced. With the motor running, pour in the oil in a very thin stream, adding the lemon juice and iced water a spoonful at a time between additions of oil. After 6–8 minutes it should be thick, white and fluffy, like mayonnaise. If it splits and turns runny, blend a fresh clove of garlic and slowly add the broken mixture back in.
Heat the grill or griddle pan until very hot. Thread the chicken onto the skewers, leaving a little space between the pieces so they cook evenly, and let excess marinade drip off.
Grill for 10–12 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes, until charred at the edges, juicy and cooked through to 74 °C in the thickest piece. Rest for 3 minutes.
Warm the pitas on the grill for a few seconds per side.
Serve the skewers with the toum, tomatoes, lettuce, pickles and pita, or slide the chicken off into the bread with a thick smear of toum and roll it up as a sandwich.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Toum keeps for 2 weeks in a sealed jar in the fridge and is also served with roast chicken and shawarma.

recipes.name: Manakish za'atar (za'atar and olive oil flatbreads)
recipes.description: Soft, chewy flatbreads dimpled and spread with za'atar mixed with olive oil, baked very hot. Lebanon's everyday breakfast, eaten folded with tomato, cucumber, mint and olives.
equipment: Baking stone, steel or heavy baking tray

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl, then add the water and olive oil and bring together. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes, until smooth, elastic and slightly tacky. Put it back in the oiled bowl, cover and leave somewhere warm for 1–1½ hours, until doubled.
Stir the za'atar and olive oil together into a loose, spreadable paste and leave it to soak for 10 minutes so the herbs soften.
Put the baking stone or tray on the top shelf and heat the oven to 250 °C (or its highest setting) for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 6 balls and rest them under a cloth for 10 minutes. Roll or press each into a round about 20 cm across and 5 mm thick, then press your fingertips all over the surface to dimple it, leaving a 1 cm rim; the dimples hold the topping in place.
Spread about 2 tablespoons of the za'atar oil over each round, right up to the rim.

Slide two at a time onto the hot stone and bake for 6–8 minutes, until the base is golden and crisp and the rim puffed and lightly browned. Watch closely at the end: za'atar darkens and turns bitter quickly.
Serve warm, folded in half or rolled around slices of tomato and cucumber, mint leaves and olives, with a glass of sweet tea.

recipes.storage: Best fresh. Wrap cooled leftovers for up to 1 day, or freeze for a month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a hot oven or dry frying pan for 2–3 minutes.
notes: For manakish jibneh, top with grated akkawi cheese or a mix of mozzarella and feta instead of za'atar.

recipes.name: Mouhalabieh (orange blossom milk pudding)
recipes.description: A silky, delicate milk pudding thickened with cornflour and scented with orange blossom and rose water, set in small bowls and topped with ground pistachios.

ingredients.name: Honey or rose syrup, to drizzle

steps.t: Whisk the cornflour with 250 ml of the cold milk in a jug until completely smooth, with no lumps at all.

Put the rest of the milk and the sugar in the heavy saucepan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves and the milk is steaming, with small bubbles around the edge, about 5 minutes. Don't let it boil over.

Whisk the cornflour mixture again and pour it into the hot milk in a steady stream, whisking constantly. Keep stirring with the spatula over medium-low heat, scraping the base and corners, for 8–10 minutes, until it thickens to a heavy custard. Once it starts to bubble slowly, cook for 2 minutes more to remove any raw starch taste.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the orange blossom water and rose water; add them gradually and taste, as brands vary in strength.
Pour into the bowls or glasses and leave to cool for 15 minutes, then cover and refrigerate for at least 3 hours, until set and cold.
Just before serving, scatter with the ground pistachios and add a thin drizzle of honey or rose syrup if you like.

recipes.storage: @chilled

recipes.name: Hummus bil lahme (hummus with spiced lamb and pine nuts)
recipes.description: Warm, freshly whipped hummus topped with sizzling minced lamb, allspice, cinnamon and toasted pine nuts in their buttery juices. A mezze favourite that makes a meal with bread and salad.

steps.t: Put the chickpeas in the saucepan, cover with fresh water and simmer for 10 minutes, until very soft; warm, soft chickpeas whip into much smoother hummus. Drain, keeping a cupful of the water, and set aside a spoonful of whole chickpeas for the garnish.

While still hot, blend the chickpeas with the garlic, lemon juice and salt for 1 minute. Add the tahini and cumin and keep blending for 3 minutes, adding the iced water a spoonful at a time (and some cooking water if needed), until pale, fluffy and very smooth. Taste for salt and lemon.

For the topping, heat the butter and oil in the frying pan over medium heat and toast the pine nuts for 2 minutes, stirring, until golden; lift them out. Add the onion and cook for 3–4 minutes until soft.

Turn the heat to high, add the lamb and cook for 6–8 minutes, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned, crisp in places and with no pink left. Season with the allspice, cinnamon, salt and pepper and stir the pine nuts back in.

Spread the hummus over two plates or a platter, making a deep well in the centre with the back of a spoon. Spoon the hot lamb and its juices into the well, then finish with the whole chickpeas, olive oil, parsley and a dusting of paprika.
Serve immediately, while the meat is sizzling and the hummus is warm, with warm pita for scooping, pickles and a chopped salad.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftover hummus and meat separately for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the lamb in a hot pan until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F); serve the hummus at room temperature.

recipes.name: Muhammara (roasted red pepper and walnut dip)
recipes.description: Aleppo's smoky-sweet dip of charred red peppers, toasted walnuts, breadcrumbs, pomegranate molasses and Aleppo pepper, with a gentle heat. Eaten with bread or alongside grilled meat.

ingredients.name: Dry breadcrumbs (or toasted crumbs from stale bread)
Aleppo pepper (pul biber), or 1 tsp chilli flakes

steps.t: Heat the oven grill to high and grill the whole peppers close to the element, turning every few minutes, for 12–15 minutes, until blackened and blistered all over (or char them over a gas flame). Put them in a bowl, cover with a plate and leave for 10 minutes, then peel, remove the stems and seeds and pat dry.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 3–4 minutes, until fragrant, and leave to cool.

Pulse the walnuts, breadcrumbs, garlic, cumin, Aleppo pepper and salt in the food processor to coarse crumbs. Add the peppers, pepper paste, pomegranate molasses and lemon juice and pulse to a thick paste that still has some texture. With the motor running, pour in 3 tablespoons of the olive oil.

Taste and balance it: it should be sweet, sour, smoky and gently hot, so add more molasses, lemon, salt or pepper as needed. Leave for at least 30 minutes for the flavours to come together (it is even better the next day), then spread on a plate, drizzle with the rest of the oil and garnish with chopped walnuts and parsley. Serve with warm pita and raw vegetables.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 5 days.

recipes.name: Fatteh hummus (chickpeas and toasted bread with yogurt and pine nuts)
recipes.description: Layers of crisp toasted bread, warm cumin-scented chickpeas and garlicky yogurt-tahini sauce, crowned with pine nuts fried in butter. A Damascus Friday breakfast eaten from a shared dish.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Toss the torn bread with the olive oil on the baking tray and bake for 8–10 minutes, until golden and crisp. (Frying the pieces is the traditional, richer way.)
Meanwhile, put the chickpeas in the saucepan with the water, cumin and salt and simmer for 10 minutes, until very hot and soft. Keep them warm in their liquid.
Whisk the yogurt, tahini, garlic, lemon juice and salt together until smooth. The yogurt should not be fridge-cold, or the dish will be lukewarm.
Melt the butter in the small pan over medium heat and fry the pine nuts for 1–2 minutes, stirring, until golden. Take off the heat and stir in the paprika.

Assemble just before eating: spread the bread in the serving dish and spoon over a few tablespoons of the hot chickpea liquid to soften it slightly. Spoon the chickpeas over, keeping a few back, then cover with the yogurt sauce.

Pour the sizzling butter and pine nuts over the top, scatter with the reserved chickpeas, a pinch of cumin and the parsley and serve at once, while the contrast of hot and cold, crisp and soft is at its best.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; the bread goes soggy on standing.
notes: Fatteh with chicken or aubergine is made the same way for lunch.

recipes.name: Ma'amoul (date-filled semolina cookies)
recipes.description: Tender, crumbly semolina cookies scented with orange blossom and rose water, filled with spiced date paste and pressed in carved wooden moulds. Baked for Eid and Easter across the Levant.
equipment: Ma'amoul mould (or a fork for decorating)
Baking trays lined with baking paper

steps.t: Put the semolina and flour in the bowl, pour over the melted ghee and rub it in with your fingertips for 3–4 minutes, until every grain is coated and the mixture feels like damp sand. Cover and leave at room temperature for at least 6 hours or overnight; this resting makes the cookies melt in the mouth.

Add the sugar, baking powder, orange blossom water, rose water and milk and knead briefly, just until it comes together into a soft dough that holds its shape when squeezed. Don't overwork it. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, warm the dates with the butter and cinnamon in the small saucepan over low heat for 2–3 minutes, mashing with a fork, until they form a smooth paste. Cool, then roll into 24 balls of about 12 g each.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Take a 30 g piece of dough, roll it into a ball and press your thumb into it, working the dough around into a thin-walled cup. Put a date ball inside and pinch the dough closed over it, then roll gently into a ball again.

Press each ball firmly into the floured mould, level the base and knock it out with a sharp tap on the work surface. Without a mould, flatten each ball slightly and decorate the top with a fork or tweezers. Arrange on the lined trays 2 cm apart.
Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the bases are golden; the tops should stay pale, which is correct. Leave to cool completely on the trays, as they are fragile while warm.
Dust with icing sugar and serve with Arabic coffee or mint tea.

recipes.storage: Keep airtight at room temperature for up to 2 weeks, or freeze for 3 months.
notes: Fill some with chopped walnuts or pistachios mixed with sugar and rose water; families use differently shaped moulds so each filling can be told apart.

recipes.name: Musakhan (sumac chicken and onions on taboon bread)
recipes.description: Roast chicken spiced with sumac and allspice, served on flatbread spread thickly with onions slowly cooked in olive oil and sumac, then baked until the bread edges crisp. Palestine's olive harvest feast.

ingredients.name: Taboon bread or other thick flatbreads (or large pitas)

steps.t: Mix the sumac, allspice, cinnamon, cardamom, salt, pepper and olive oil and rub all over the chicken pieces, getting some under the skin. Leave for 30 minutes at room temperature, or refrigerate overnight.

Heat the oven to 200 °C. Arrange the chicken skin side up in the roasting tin and roast for 45–50 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and the thickest part of a thigh reaches 74 °C with clear juices. Keep the juices in the tin.

Meanwhile, heat the 90 ml of olive oil in the large frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the onions and salt and cook gently, stirring often, for 25–30 minutes, until very soft, sweet and translucent; they should not brown. Stir in the 4 tablespoons of sumac: the onions turn a deep purple-red.
Brush the flatbreads with some of the chicken juices and oil from the roasting tin and set them on the baking trays.
Spread a thick layer of sumac onions over each bread and set the chicken pieces on top. Scatter with the toasted pine nuts and a little more sumac, and drizzle with the remaining pan juices.
Return to the oven for 8–10 minutes, until the edges of the bread are crisp and the chicken is sizzling.
Serve hot, with yogurt and a chopped salad. Musakhan is eaten with the hands: tear off bread soaked with onion and olive oil to wrap each bite of chicken.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: For musakhan rolls, shred the chicken, mix with the onions and roll in thin flatbread before baking until crisp.

recipes.name: Maqluba (upside-down rice with chicken, aubergine and cauliflower)
recipes.description: Layers of fried aubergine and cauliflower, chicken and spiced rice cooked in one pot in chicken stock, then flipped onto a platter to reveal a domed cake. A Friday family dish with a dramatic unveiling.
equipment: Large heavy non-stick pot (26 cm, at least 5 litres)
Deep pan or wok for frying

ingredients.name: Chicken legs or thighs, bone-in and skinless
Aubergines (2 medium)
ingredients.prep: cut into 1.5 cm rounds and salted

steps.t: Put the chicken in the large saucepan with the water, halved onion, cinnamon stick, cardamom, bay leaves, allspice and salt. Bring to the boil, skim off the foam, then simmer for 30 minutes, until the chicken is just cooked. Lift out the chicken, strain the stock and keep it hot; you need about 900 ml.

While the stock cooks, salt the aubergine slices for 20 minutes, then pat them dry. Heat the oil in the deep pan to 175 °C and fry the aubergine in batches for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden. Fry the cauliflower for 5–6 minutes, until golden brown at the edges. Drain everything on kitchen paper. (To roast instead, brush with oil and bake at 220 °C for 25 minutes.)

Line the base of the heavy pot with the tomato slices; they stop the rice sticking and look pretty when turned out. Arrange the chicken over them, then the aubergine and cauliflower in snug layers, tucking the garlic cloves in between.

Drain the rice, toss it with the turmeric, allspice, cinnamon and pepper and spread it evenly over the vegetables, pressing down gently. Pour in hot stock until it covers the rice by about 2 cm, then lay a small plate on top to hold the layers in place.

Bring to the boil, cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 30–35 minutes, until the rice is tender and the stock has been absorbed. Take off the heat and leave covered, untouched, for 15 minutes; this rest lets it hold its shape when turned out.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a small pan and fry the almonds and pine nuts for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until golden.

Remove the lid and plate. Place the platter upside down over the pot and, holding both firmly with oven gloves, flip them over in one confident movement. Wait a minute, then lift the pot away slowly to reveal the maqluba ('upside down'). Scatter with the nuts and parsley and serve with yogurt and a chopped salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Msabbaha (warm chickpeas in tahini with garlic-lemon sauce)
recipes.description: Hummus's rustic cousin: soft, warm whole chickpeas folded through lemony tahini and topped with a sharp garlic, chilli and cumin sauce and olive oil. A favourite Jerusalem breakfast.

steps.t: Simmer the chickpeas in the water for 10–12 minutes, until very soft and hot all the way through. Drain, keeping about 150 ml of the cooking water.
While they cook, make the dakka: pound the garlic, chilli and salt in the mortar to a coarse paste, then stir in the lemon juice and cumin.
Mash about a quarter of the hot chickpeas in the bowl with the tahini, lemon juice, salt and a few tablespoons of the cooking water until it forms a loose, creamy sauce.
Fold in the remaining whole chickpeas with more cooking water as needed, so the msabbaha is spoonable and slightly soupy rather than stiff. Taste for salt and lemon.
Spoon into shallow bowls while warm. Top with the dakka, a generous pour of olive oil, parsley and a dusting of paprika.
Serve straight away with warm pita, raw onion wedges, pickles and fresh mint tea.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water until hot throughout.

recipes.name: Mansaf (lamb in yogurt sauce with rice)
recipes.description: Jordan's national feast: lamb simmered until tender, then finished in a tangy yogurt sauce, served on thin bread and turmeric rice with toasted almonds and pine nuts, and plenty of extra sauce to pour over.

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or leg, in large pieces
ingredients.prep: boneless weight (bone-in pieces are traditional; use about 1.6 kg)

ingredients.name: Full-fat yogurt (or liquid jameed, see notes)

steps.t: Put the lamb in the stockpot, cover with the cold water and bring to the boil. Boil for 10 minutes, skimming off all the grey scum that rises, until the surface is clear.
Add the onion, cardamom, bay leaves, peppercorns, cinnamon stick and salt. Cover and simmer gently for 1½–2 hours, until the lamb is very tender. Lift out the meat and strain the broth.

For the sauce, whisk the yogurt and cornflour in the heavy pot until completely smooth; the cornflour stops it splitting. Set over medium heat and stir constantly in one direction with the wooden spoon for 10–15 minutes, until it comes to a gentle bubble. Then gradually stir in about 750 ml of the hot lamb broth until the sauce is the consistency of single cream.
Add the lamb to the sauce and simmer gently for 20–30 minutes, so the meat takes on the tangy flavour. Taste for salt.

Meanwhile, melt 3 tablespoons of ghee in the lidded saucepan, stir in the turmeric and the drained rice and stir for 2 minutes until coated. Add 900 ml of the lamb broth (topped up with water if needed) and the salt, bring to the boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 18–20 minutes. Rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
Toast the almonds and pine nuts in the remaining tablespoon of ghee over medium heat for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until golden.

Lay the bread over the serving tray and moisten it with a few ladles of sauce. Heap the rice on top, arrange the lamb over it and scatter with the nuts and parsley. Serve the rest of the sauce in bowls for everyone to pour over. Traditionally mansaf is eaten standing around the tray, with the right hand.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat the lamb in its sauce gently, stirring, until steaming hot (74 °C / 165 °F); reheat the rice separately.
notes: The authentic sauce uses jameed, dried salted fermented yogurt from Jordan's Karak region, soaked and blended with water; it is saltier and sharper, so season after adding it. Liquid jameed is sold in cartons in Middle Eastern shops.

recipes.name: Masgouf (Iraqi butterflied fish, oven-roasted)
recipes.description: Baghdad's riverside favourite: whole fish split open, rubbed with turmeric, tamarind and oil and roasted until smoky at the edges, then topped with tomato and onion. Adapted here for a hot home oven.

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass or carp (1.5 kg in total, 1 large or 2 small)

steps.t: Butterfly the fish, or ask your fishmonger to: cut along the back from head to tail, close to the backbone, and open it out flat like a book so it stays joined along the belly. Rinse and pat completely dry.
Mix the oil, tamarind, turmeric, curry powder, salt and pepper into a paste and rub it all over the flesh side. Leave for 20 minutes while the oven heats.
Heat the oven to 240 °C with a shelf near the top. Lay the fish skin side down on the lined tray, opened out flat.
Roast for 15 minutes, until the flesh has turned opaque and the edges are starting to colour.

Scatter the onion rings, tomato and pepper slices over the fish, drizzle with a little more oil and roast for 10–12 minutes more. Finish under a hot grill for 3–5 minutes for charred spots, until the flesh flakes easily at the thickest part (63 °C).
Bring the fish to the table on its tray with the flatbreads, lemon wedges and parsley. Everyone pulls the flesh off the bones with pieces of bread; serve with pickles and a chopped salad.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftovers off the bone for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, covered, in a low oven until hot throughout.
notes: On the banks of the Tigris, carp is impaled on stakes and slow-cooked beside a wood fire; a charcoal grill with a hinged fish basket gives the closest result.

recipes.name: Iraqi kebab (lamb kebab with parsley and onion)
recipes.description: Juicy kebabs of minced lamb and beef with onion and parsley, grilled on flat skewers and wrapped in warm bread with grilled tomatoes, sumac onions and pickles, as in Baghdad's kebab shops.

steps.t: Grate the onion finely and squeeze it hard in the tea towel to remove as much juice as possible; discard the juice.

Put both meats in the bowl with the onion, parsley, garlic, baharat, salt and pepper. Knead for 4–5 minutes, until the mixture is sticky and holds together in one mass. Chill for 20–30 minutes if you have time; firm meat is easier to shape.
Light the charcoal and let it burn to glowing coals, or heat the oven grill to high. For the onion salad, toss the sliced onion with the sumac, parsley leaves and a pinch of salt.
Divide the meat into 8 portions. With wet hands, press each around a skewer into a kebab about 2 cm thick, squeezing it along the skewer so it holds tightly, and pinch the ends firmly onto the metal.
Grill for 8–10 minutes, turning every 2 minutes, until browned on all sides, juicy and cooked through to 71 °C. Grill the tomatoes alongside until soft and blackened in spots.

Warm the breads on the grill, then use one to pull the kebabs off each skewer. Serve wrapped in the bread with grilled tomatoes, sumac onions and pickles; amba (mango pickle sauce) is the classic Iraqi addition.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Chicken kabsa (Saudi spiced chicken and rice)
recipes.description: Saudi Arabia's everyday feast: chicken simmered with tomato, dried lime and warm whole spices, then long-grain rice cooked in the fragrant broth and heaped on a platter with fried almonds and raisins.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

steps.t: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then leave it to soak in fresh water for 30 minutes while you cook the chicken.
Heat 4 tablespoons of oil in the large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken pieces on all sides for about 8 minutes, in two batches if needed, then lift them out.

Add the onions to the pot and cook for 8 minutes, until golden. Add the garlic and chillies for 1 minute, then the whole spices for 30 seconds until fragrant, then the ground spices and tomato paste for 1 minute. Stir in the grated tomatoes and carrot and cook for 5 minutes, until thick and jammy.
Return the chicken, add the dried limes, water and salt and bring to the boil. Cover and simmer for 30 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through to 74 °C.

Lift out the chicken. For crisp skin, brush it with oil and roast at 220 °C for 10–12 minutes while the rice cooks. Measure the broth: you need about 900 ml for 600 g of rice, so boil it down or top it up with water.

Bring the broth to the boil, add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 5 minutes, until the liquid has dropped to the level of the rice. Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and every grain separate. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, fry the almonds and raisins in 1 tablespoon of oil in the small frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, until the almonds are golden and the raisins puffed.

Heap the rice on the platter, removing the whole spices as you find them, set the chicken on top and scatter with the almonds and raisins. Serve with a tomato and cucumber salad, yogurt and a hot tomato and chilli sauce (daqoos).

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Lamb kabsa is made the same way: simmer lamb pieces for 1½ hours before adding the rice.

recipes.name: Chicken machboos (Gulf spiced rice with chicken and hashu)
recipes.description: The Gulf's signature rice: chicken cooked with deeply browned onions, bzar spices and dried limes, rice steamed in the broth with saffron and rose water, topped with sweet caramelised onions, chickpeas and raisins.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

steps.t: Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee in the large pot over medium heat and fry the onions, stirring often, for 10–12 minutes, until a deep golden brown; this colour gives machboos its depth. Add the garlic, ginger and chillies for 1 minute, then the bzar, turmeric and whole spices for 30 seconds.

Add the chicken and turn it in the spiced onions for 5 minutes. Add the tomatoes, dried limes, water and salt, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 35–40 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through to 74 °C.

Meanwhile, make the hashu: cook the sliced onion in 1 tablespoon of ghee in the frying pan over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, stirring, until soft and caramelised. Add the chickpeas, raisins, sugar, ground cardamom and 2 tablespoons of water and cook for 5 minutes, until glossy and sticky.
Lift the chicken out of the pot and keep it warm (or brown it under a hot grill for 5 minutes). Measure the broth, boiling it down or adding water to make about 900 ml, and bring it back to the boil.

Add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 5–6 minutes, until the liquid is level with the rice and small steam holes appear. Drizzle the saffron water, rose water and 1 tablespoon of ghee over the top, cover with a lid wrapped in the tea towel and cook on the lowest heat for 20–25 minutes, until the rice is tender and fluffy.

Spoon the rice onto a large platter, mixing the saffron streaks lightly, arrange the chicken on top and spoon over the hashu. Scatter with coriander and serve with salad, yogurt and daqoos (tomato and chilli sauce).

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Chicken mandi (Yemeni roast chicken on smoky rice)
recipes.description: Spice-rubbed chicken roasted above a tray of basmati so its juices drip into the rice, then smoked briefly with a glowing coal. A Hadhrami dish traditionally cooked in an underground oven, adapted for a home oven.
equipment: Wire rack that fits over the tin

steps.t: Mix the ground spices, garlic, salt and oil into a paste and rub it all over the chicken, under the skin as well. Leave for at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 200 °C. Set the roasting tin over medium heat on the hob, add 2 tablespoons of oil and cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add the whole spices for 1 minute, then the drained rice, and stir for 2 minutes until coated.

Pour in the hot stock, add the dried limes and salt and bring to the boil. Set the rack over the tin and lay the chicken on it, skin side up, so its juices will drip onto the rice. Cover the whole tin tightly with foil.

Bake for 50 minutes. Uncover, brush the chicken with the melted ghee and turn the oven up to 220 °C. Roast for 20–25 minutes more, until the skin is deep golden, the thickest part of the thigh reaches 74 °C and the rice is tender, with crisp edges.

For the classic smoky flavour (optional), heat a piece of lump charcoal over a gas flame with tongs for 5–7 minutes until glowing. Set it in the small heatproof bowl in the middle of the rice, drop 1 teaspoon of ghee onto it and cover the tin tightly with foil for 10 minutes. Remove the coal carefully and do this only in a well-ventilated kitchen.
Fluff the rice, heap it onto a platter with the chicken on top and scatter with the almonds and raisins. Serve with zhug or a fresh tomato-chilli salsa and a green salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Saltah (Yemeni lamb stew with whipped fenugreek)
recipes.description: Yemen's national dish: a spicy, bubbling stew of lamb broth, potatoes, tomatoes and chilli brought to the table in a scorching pot and crowned with frothy whipped fenugreek (hulba).

ingredients.name: Ground fenugreek
ingredients.prep: soaked in 250 ml water for at least 4 hours

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander
ingredients.prep: pounded with the chilli and garlic

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1.5 cm dice

steps.t: Start the hulba ahead: soak the ground fenugreek in 250 ml of water for at least 4 hours or overnight. The soaking draws out its bitterness; pour off the water before using.

For the broth, put the lamb in the stockpot with the water, halved onion, cardamom, peppercorns, turmeric and salt. Bring to the boil, skim, then simmer covered for about 1 hour, until the lamb is tender. Lift out the meat and shred it, and strain the broth.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the chopped onion for 6 minutes, until golden. Add the garlic, chillies, cumin and coriander for 1 minute, then the tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes, until soft.

Add the potatoes and about 500 ml of the broth and simmer for 15 minutes, until the potatoes are tender. Stir in the shredded lamb and mash a few potato pieces against the pan to thicken the stew. It should be thick but loose enough to bubble. Season with salt.

Whip the hulba: put the drained fenugreek in a bowl with 2–3 tablespoons of cold water and whisk hard for 5–8 minutes, adding cold water a spoonful at a time, until it turns pale, frothy and roughly doubles in volume. Pound the coriander, chilli, garlic and salt to a paste and whisk it in with the lemon juice.
Heat the cast-iron or stone pot over high heat until very hot. Tip in the stew so it boils fiercely, then spoon the hulba on top and carry it bubbling to the table.
Eat straight from the pot, scooping up the stew and froth with torn flatbread, with cups of the remaining hot broth to drink alongside.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the stew and broth within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; whip the hulba fresh.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Some cooks crack an egg or two into the bubbling stew just before adding the hulba.

recipes.name: Zhug (Yemeni green chilli and herb sauce)
recipes.description: A fiery green paste of fresh chillies, coriander, garlic, cumin and cardamom, called sahawiq in Yemen. Spooned onto stews, eggs, falafel, grilled meat and rice.
equipment: Food processor or large mortar and pestle

steps.t: For a milder zhug, scrape out some of the chilli seeds and white membranes before chopping. Wear gloves or wash your hands well afterwards.

Pulse the chillies, garlic, cumin, cardamom, black pepper and salt in the food processor until coarsely chopped, scraping down the sides. Traditionally it is pounded on a stone, which gives a slightly coarser paste.
Add the coriander and parsley and pulse until finely chopped but not completely smooth; you want some texture. Add the olive oil and lemon juice and pulse briefly to combine.
Taste and adjust the salt and lemon, then leave for 15 minutes for the flavours to blend. Serve with saltah, mandi, eggs, falafel or grilled meat, or stir a spoonful into yogurt as a dip.

recipes.storage: Keep in a jar under a thin layer of olive oil in the fridge for up to 1 week, or freeze in small portions.
notes: Red zhug is made the same way with red chillies.

recipes.name: Luqaimat (crisp dumplings with date syrup)
recipes.description: Small yeasted dumplings scented with cardamom and saffron, fried until crisp outside and airy within, then drizzled with date syrup and sesame. Made every evening in Ramadan across the Gulf.

steps.t: Whisk the flour, cornflour, yeast, sugar, salt and cardamom in the bowl. Add the saffron water, milk and water and beat with the whisk or a wooden spoon for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, thick, sticky batter, a little thicker than pancake batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled and full of bubbles. Stir it down briefly just before frying.
Pour the oil into the deep pan to about 6 cm deep, no more than one-third full, and heat to 170 °C on the thermometer.
