Dip the two teaspoons in a cup of oil, scoop up a walnut-sized blob of batter with one and push it off into the oil with the other. (In Emirati homes the batter is squeezed out between thumb and forefinger.) Fry 10–12 at a time without crowding.

Fry for 5–7 minutes, turning them constantly with the slotted spoon so they colour evenly, until deep golden brown and crisp. They should sound hollow and feel light. Drain on a rack or kitchen paper and let the oil come back to 170 °C between batches.
While still hot, drizzle with the date syrup, toss to coat and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Serve immediately with Arabic coffee or karak chai; they are at their best within the hour.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within an hour; they soften as they stand.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes, then add the syrup.
notes: Sugar syrup flavoured with saffron and cardamom, or honey, can replace the date syrup.

recipes.name: Karak chai (strong cardamom tea with evaporated milk)
recipes.description: Black tea boiled hard with cardamom until strong ('karak'), then simmered with evaporated milk and sugar into a rich caramel-coloured brew. Sold from roadside cafeterias all over the Gulf.

ingredients.name: Strong loose black tea (or 4 tea bags)

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil in the saucepan with the crushed cardamom (and saffron, if using) and boil for 3 minutes, so the cardamom flavours the water.
Add the tea and boil hard for 3–4 minutes, until the liquid is very dark, almost black; this long boil is what makes it karak, or strong.

Stir in the evaporated milk and sugar and bring back to the boil over medium heat. Watch closely: as it rises, lift the pan off the heat or lower it, let the foam settle, then bring it up again. Repeat 2–3 times over 3–4 minutes, until the tea is a deep caramel colour and slightly thickened.
Pour through the strainer into small glasses or cups and serve very hot, with luqaimat, biscuits or a chapati sandwich.

recipes.storage: Best made fresh.

recipes.name: Balaleet (sweet saffron vermicelli with omelette)
recipes.description: Toasted vermicelli sweetened with sugar, cardamom, saffron and rose water, topped with a thin savoury omelette. A sweet-and-salty Emirati breakfast, also served on Eid mornings.
equipment: Non-stick frying pan with a lid

steps.t: Stir the rose water into the steeped saffron and set aside.

Melt 2 tablespoons of ghee in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the broken vermicelli and stir constantly for 3–4 minutes, until evenly golden brown and smelling nutty; it can burn quickly at the end.
Carefully pour in the boiling water (it will spit), stir and cook for 3–4 minutes, until the vermicelli is just tender. If much water remains, pour it off.

Stir in the sugar, cardamom and saffron-rose water and cook over low heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring gently, until the sugar has dissolved and the vermicelli is glossy and golden. Cover and keep warm off the heat.

Whisk the eggs with the salt (and a few saffron threads for colour if you like). Melt the remaining ghee in the frying pan over medium-low heat, pour in the eggs and cook, covered, for 3–4 minutes, until set right through. Slide out and cut into wedges or strips.
Spoon the warm vermicelli into bowls, lay the omelette on top and scatter with pistachios. Serve with sweet tea or karak chai.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; the vermicelli keeps 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the vermicelli with a splash of water until hot; make the omelette fresh.

recipes.name: Plov (Uzbek lamb, carrot and rice pilaf)
recipes.description: Uzbekistan's national dish, called osh at home: lamb and a mountain of carrot matchsticks slowly cooked with cumin into a rich base (zirvak), then rice steamed on top with whole heads of garlic buried inside.
equipment: Heavy cast-iron pot or kazan (6 litres) with a lid

ingredients.name: Carrots (yellow and orange)
ingredients.prep: cut into 5 mm matchsticks, not grated

ingredients.name: Medium-grain rice (devzira or Calrose)
ingredients.prep: rinsed and soaked in warm salted water for 1 hour

ingredients.name: Whole heads of garlic (2)
ingredients.prep: loose papery skin rubbed off, left whole

steps.t: Rinse the rice in several changes of water until it runs clear and soak it in warm salted water for 1 hour. Cut the carrots into long matchsticks by hand; grated carrot turns to mush.

Heat the oil in the kazan over high heat until it shimmers and just starts to smoke. Fry the lamb in two batches, turning, for 8–10 minutes, until a deep brown crust forms on all sides. Return all the meat to the pot.

Add the onions and fry for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until golden brown. Spread the carrots over the top in a thick layer and leave them for 2–3 minutes without stirring, then stir and fry for 10 minutes more, until softened, glossy and turning golden.

Rub the cumin seeds between your palms over the pot to release their aroma, then add the coriander, whole chillies, barberries, drained chickpeas and 2 teaspoons of the salt. Pour in enough boiling water to just cover, bring to the boil and simmer gently, partly covered, for 45–60 minutes, until the lamb is tender. This rich base is the zirvak.

Turn the heat up. Drain the rice and spread it evenly over the zirvak without stirring. Pour boiling water gently over the back of the slotted spoon so the rice is not disturbed, until it is covered by about 1.5 cm. Add the remaining salt and press the whole garlic heads into the centre of the rice.

Boil hard, uncovered, for 10–12 minutes, until the water has sunk below the surface of the rice. Gather the rice into a dome with the slotted spoon and poke 6–8 holes down to the bottom with the handle of a wooden spoon so steam can rise.
Cover tightly (a plate under the lid helps) and cook on the lowest heat for 25–30 minutes, until the rice is tender and fluffy. Turn off the heat and rest for 10 minutes without lifting the lid.

Fold the rice and carrots together gently from the sides, then heap them on the platter. Arrange the lamb and the soft garlic heads on top. Serve with achichuk (sliced tomato, onion and chilli salad), non bread and green tea.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Some regions add raisins or quince; in Samarkand the layers are not mixed before serving.

recipes.name: Samsa (Uzbek flaky lamb and onion pastries)
recipes.description: Triangular pastries of buttery, spiral-layered dough filled with diced lamb, plenty of onion, cumin and black pepper, baked until shatteringly flaky. Sold hot from tandoor ovens across Central Asia.
equipment: Baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder with some of its fat
ingredients.prep: cut into 5 mm dice (or coarse lamb mince)

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt with the cold water and knead for 8–10 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes so it relaxes and rolls out thinly.

Roll the dough out on a lightly floured surface as thinly as you can, into a rectangle about 50 × 60 cm. Spread the soft butter over the whole surface, then roll it up tightly from a long side into a log. Cut it into 12 pieces, wrap and chill for 30 minutes to firm the butter; this creates the flaky spiral layers.
For the filling, mix the diced lamb with the onions, crushed cumin, pepper, salt and cold water. The filling goes in raw; the onion juices keep it moist as it bakes.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Stand each piece of dough on a cut side and press it flat with your palm so the spiral faces up, then roll it into a 12–13 cm round, thinner at the edges than in the centre.

Put 2 heaped tablespoons of filling in the centre. Fold three sides up over the filling to meet in the middle, forming a triangle, and pinch the seams tightly closed. Set seam side down on the lined trays.
Brush with the beaten egg, sprinkle with sesame or nigella seeds and bake for 25–30 minutes, until deep golden and flaky and the filling is sizzling; the centre of the filling should reach 71 °C.
Cool for 5 minutes, as the juices inside are very hot, and serve warm with green tea and a tomato and onion salad.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; unbaked samsa freeze well (bake from frozen, adding 10 minutes).
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 10–12 minutes until hot throughout; a microwave makes the pastry soft.
notes: Pumpkin samsa (with diced squash, onion and a little butter) is the autumn vegetarian version.

recipes.name: Laghman (Uyghur hand-pulled noodles with lamb and vegetables)
recipes.description: Springy hand-pulled noodles topped with a stir-fried sauce of lamb, peppers, celery, green beans and tomato, seasoned with cumin, garlic and black vinegar. The great noodle dish of the Uyghurs.

steps.t: Dissolve the salt and bicarbonate of soda in the water and mix it into the flour to a shaggy dough. Knead for 10 minutes, rest it covered for 20 minutes, then knead again for 5 minutes, until very smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 30 minutes more; the long rests relax the gluten so the noodles stretch without snapping.

Divide the dough into 12–16 pieces and roll each into a rope as thick as a pencil and about 15 cm long. Coat them well with oil, coil them on the oiled plate, cover with cling film and rest for at least 30 minutes, or up to 2 hours.

For the topping, heat the oil in the wok over high heat and stir-fry the lamb for 2–3 minutes, until browned. Add the onion and garlic for 2 minutes, then the cumin and tomato paste for 1 minute. Add the peppers, celery, beans and chilli and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, soy sauce, salt and water and simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the vegetables are tender-crisp and the sauce has thickened and turned glossy. Stir in the vinegar and keep warm.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Pick up a rope by both ends and stretch it gently, bouncing the middle on the work surface, until it is 1–1.5 metres long and 3–4 mm thick; loop it around your hands and keep stretching if it is still thick. Drop it straight into the boiling water and repeat with the rest, working in batches.
Boil for 2–3 minutes, until the noodles float and are tender but chewy. Lift them into a bowl of cold water for a few seconds to firm them, then drain and toss with a few drops of oil.
Divide the noodles between bowls and ladle the hot lamb and vegetable sauce over them. Serve with more vinegar, crushed garlic and chilli oil at the table.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the sauce and noodles separately within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the sauce until steaming hot throughout; dip the noodles in boiling water for 30 seconds.
notes: Short of time, use 500 g of fresh thick wheat noodles or dried lamian noodles instead of pulling your own.

recipes.name: Shurpa (Uzbek lamb and vegetable soup)
recipes.description: A clear, golden lamb broth with large pieces of meat, potatoes, carrots, peppers, tomatoes and chickpeas, finished with dill and coriander. Simple, restorative Central Asian home cooking.

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or neck
ingredients.prep: in large pieces (bone-in pieces are traditional)

steps.t: Put the lamb in the stockpot with the cold water and bring slowly to the boil over medium heat. As it comes up, skim off all the grey foam for about 10 minutes, until the surface is clean; this keeps the broth clear.

Add the drained chickpeas, the whole onion, the bay leaves and peppercorns. Lower the heat so the broth barely trembles and simmer, partly covered, for 1–1½ hours, until the lamb is tender. Hard boiling makes the broth cloudy.
Remove and discard the whole onion. Add the carrots, pepper, tomatoes and sliced onion and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the potatoes, cumin, ground coriander and salt and simmer for 20 minutes more, until the potatoes are tender but still whole.
Lift out the lamb, cut it into portions and return it to the pot with the garlic and whole chilli. Simmer for 5 minutes and taste for salt.
Ladle into deep bowls so everyone gets a piece of meat, potato and vegetables. Scatter generously with dill and coriander and serve with non bread and thinly sliced raw onion.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days, or freeze the broth for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Sabich (pita with fried aubergine, egg and tahini)
recipes.description: Pita stuffed with fried aubergine, sliced hard-boiled egg, tahini, chopped salad and tangy amba. Brought to Israel by Iraqi Jews as a Shabbat breakfast and now a beloved street sandwich.

steps.t: Sprinkle the aubergine slices with the salt and leave them in a colander for 20 minutes to draw out moisture, then pat them completely dry with kitchen paper.
Lower the eggs into a saucepan of boiling water and cook for 9–10 minutes for firm yolks. Cool them in iced water, peel and slice.

Heat about 1 cm of oil in the frying pan to 175 °C, or until a piece of aubergine sizzles at once. Fry the slices in batches for 3–4 minutes per side, until deep golden outside and creamy all the way through. Drain on kitchen paper.
Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice and garlic, then whisk in the cold water a spoonful at a time until smooth and pourable; it thickens before it loosens. Season with salt.
Mix the tomatoes, cucumber, onion and parsley with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.

Warm the pitas and open the pockets. Spread tahini inside, add a few slices of aubergine and egg and a spoonful of salad, then repeat the layers. Finish with more tahini, amba and zhug and eat straight away, with extra napkins.

recipes.storage: Assemble just before eating; fried aubergine and boiled eggs keep 2 days refrigerated.
notes: Amba, a pickled mango sauce with fenugreek and turmeric, is sold in jars in Middle Eastern shops.

recipes.name: Israeli salad (finely chopped cucumber and tomato salad)
recipes.description: Cucumbers and tomatoes diced very small and evenly, with onion and parsley, dressed simply with lemon and olive oil. Eaten at almost every Israeli meal, from breakfast to falafel.

steps.t: Cut the cucumbers and tomatoes into small, even dice about 5 mm across. The fine, uniform cut is what makes this salad; take your time and use a sharp knife so the tomatoes don't bleed.
Dice the onion as finely as you can and chop the parsley. Put everything in the bowl.
Just before serving, add the lemon juice, olive oil, salt and pepper and toss gently. Salt draws out the vegetables' juices, so don't dress it ahead.
Serve straight away, at breakfast with eggs, labneh and bread, or alongside falafel, schnitzel or sabich. A pinch of sumac or za'atar on top is a popular addition.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; undressed, the chopped vegetables keep a few hours in the fridge.

recipes.name: Jachnun (slow-baked rolled Yemenite pastry)
recipes.description: Paper-thin layers of buttery dough rolled into logs and baked overnight at a low heat until deep amber, flaky and slightly sweet. The Yemenite-Jewish Shabbat breakfast, served with grated tomato, zhug and slow-baked eggs.
equipment: Heavy ovenproof pot with a tight lid (about 24 cm)

ingredients.name: Margarine (traditional, keeps it pareve) or butter

steps.t: Mix the flour, sugar and salt in a bowl, add the water and knead for 10 minutes into a very smooth, soft, elastic dough that is slightly sticky. Divide it into 6 balls, coat each with a little margarine, cover and rest for 1 hour (or overnight in the fridge).

Grease a large work surface and your hands with margarine. Flatten a ball and stretch it outwards with your fingertips and the backs of your hands into a very thin rectangle about 50 × 40 cm, so thin that you can see the surface through it. Small tears don't matter.

Spread the sheet thinly with soft margarine. Fold the long sides in towards the middle in thirds to make a strip about 10 cm wide, spread it with a little more margarine, then roll it up tightly from a short end into a log. Repeat with the other balls.

Line the pot with baking paper and pack the logs in snugly side by side. Nestle the washed eggs in their shells between and on top of the rolls. Cover with another sheet of baking paper, then foil, then the lid, sealing tightly so no steam escapes.

Bake at 100 °C for 10 hours, overnight, or between 8 and 12 hours. The jachnun is ready when it is a deep caramel brown, crisp on the outside and flaky within; the eggs inside turn creamy with beige whites.
Serve hot from the pot with the peeled brown eggs, freshly grated tomato seasoned with a pinch of salt, and zhug for spooning over each bite.

recipes.storage: Cool, wrap and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze the shaped, unbaked logs for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Warm, covered, in a 150 °C oven for 15 minutes.
notes: Kubaneh (a domed yeasted bread) and malawach (pan-fried layered flatbread) are made from similar buttery Yemenite doughs.

recipes.name: Kabuli pulao (Afghan lamb rice with carrots and raisins)
recipes.description: Afghanistan's national dish: tender lamb hidden under rice cooked in a dark, onion-rich broth with warm spices, crowned with sweet caramelised carrot strips, raisins, almonds and pistachios.
equipment: Large heavy ovenproof pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or shank
ingredients.prep: boneless weight, in large pieces (bone-in is traditional)

ingredients.name: Aged long-grain basmati or sella rice

steps.t: Heat 6 tablespoons of oil in the heavy pot over medium heat and fry the onions, stirring often, for 12–15 minutes, until a deep, even brown; this is what gives the rice its rich colour. Don't let them blacken.

Add the lamb and brown it with the onions for 8–10 minutes. Stir in the cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, pepper and salt, pour in the water and bring to the boil. Cover and simmer for 1–1½ hours, until the lamb is tender.

Meanwhile, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the carrots for 5–7 minutes, until tender and lightly caramelised. Sprinkle with the sugar, cook for 1 minute more and lift them out. In the same pan, fry the raisins for 1–2 minutes until they puff, then the almonds and pistachios for 2 minutes until lightly toasted.

Heat the oven to 150 °C. Lift the lamb out of the pot and measure the broth: you need about 1.2 litres for 800 g of rice, so top up with water or boil it down. Bring it back to the boil, add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 6–8 minutes, until the liquid has been absorbed and small steam holes appear on the surface.

Push the lamb down into the rice, or lay it on top, and pile the carrots and raisins over the rice. Cover with a lid wrapped in the tea towel and bake for 40 minutes (or cook on the lowest heat on the hob), until the rice is tender and every grain separate.

To serve, spoon the topping aside, heap the rice on the platter with the lamb buried in the centre, and cover with the carrots, raisins and nuts. Serve with a tomato and onion salad, yogurt and green chutney.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Mantu (Afghan beef dumplings with yogurt and split pea sauce)
recipes.description: Steamed dumplings filled with spiced beef and onion, served on garlicky strained yogurt and topped with a tomato and yellow split pea sauce, dried mint and chilli. A centrepiece of Afghan celebrations.

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt, then add the egg and water and knead for 8–10 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 5 minutes until soft. Add the beef and garlic and cook for 8–10 minutes, breaking it up, until no pink remains and the liquid has evaporated. Season with the coriander, pepper and salt and leave to cool.

For the sauce, simmer the split peas in plenty of water for 25–30 minutes, until tender but holding their shape, then drain. Heat the oil in the saucepan, fry the garlic for 30 seconds, add the tomato paste and grated tomato and cook for 3 minutes. Add the split peas, chilli, salt and 200 ml of water and simmer for 10 minutes into a thick sauce.

Roll the dough out on a floured surface as thinly as you can, about 1 mm, and cut it into 8 cm squares. Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each. Bring two opposite corners up over the filling and pinch them together, then bring up the other two corners and pinch all the edges together to make a little four-cornered parcel.

Oil the steamer tiers and arrange the mantu 1 cm apart. Steam over rapidly boiling water for 25–30 minutes, until the dough is translucent and tender. (With shop-bought wonton wrappers, 12–15 minutes is enough.)
Mix the yogurt with the crushed garlic, a pinch of salt and a little water so it spreads easily.

Spread half the yogurt over a warm platter, arrange the mantu on top and spoon over the rest of the yogurt and the hot split pea sauce. Sprinkle with dried mint, chilli flakes and coriander and serve straight away.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; keep the sauces separately. Uncooked mantu freeze well on a tray.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam for 5–8 minutes until hot throughout and reheat the sauce until steaming.
notes: Many Afghan cooks use square wonton wrappers instead of homemade dough; the filling is the same.

recipes.name: Bolani (Afghan flatbread stuffed with potato and leek)
recipes.description: Thin half-moon flatbreads filled with potato mashed with leek, coriander and chilli, fried until blistered and crisp. Sold on Kabul's streets and made at home for Eid and picnics, with yogurt and chutney.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan or griddle

ingredients.name: Gandana (Afghan leek), or the white and pale green of leeks
Plain yogurt
ingredients.prep: mixed with a pinch of salt and dried mint

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt, oil and water and knead for 8 minutes into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Boil the potatoes in salted water for 15–20 minutes, until completely tender, then drain well and mash. Wash the sliced leeks thoroughly to remove grit, squeeze them dry and stir them into the hot mash with the coriander, chilli, ground coriander, salt and pepper. Leave to cool.
Divide the dough into 8 balls. Roll each out on a floured surface into a thin round about 22 cm across and 1–2 mm thick.

Spread about 4 tablespoons of filling over one half of a round, leaving a 1 cm border. Fold the other half over to make a half-moon, press out any air and seal the edge firmly with your fingers or a fork. Prick the top a few times. Keep shaped bolani under a cloth while you make the rest.

Heat the frying pan over medium-high heat with about 1 tablespoon of oil. Fry the bolani one or two at a time for 2–3 minutes per side, brushing the top with oil before turning, until golden, blistered and crisp, and the dough is cooked through.
Cut into wedges and serve hot with the minty yogurt and a green chilli and coriander chutney.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooled bolani for up to 3 days, or freeze for a month.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a dry frying pan or 200 °C oven for 4–5 minutes until hot through.
notes: A pumpkin filling (kadu) or a lentil filling are other favourites.

recipes.name: Khachapuri adjaruli (Georgian cheese boats with egg)
recipes.description: Boat-shaped yeasted breads filled with molten salty cheese, finished with a runny egg yolk and a pat of butter to stir in at the table. The famous bread of Georgia's Black Sea coast.
equipment: Baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.prep: separated: whites into the cheese, yolks kept whole

steps.t: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm milk and water and leave for 5 minutes until foamy. Add the flour, salt and oil and knead for 8–10 minutes into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.

Mix the grated sulguni or mozzarella and the crumbled cheese with the egg whites to a thick, moist paste. If your feta is very salty, soak it in cold water for 15 minutes first and squeeze it dry. Keep each yolk in its half shell or a small cup.
Put two baking trays in the oven and heat it to 240 °C. Divide the dough into 6 pieces and roll each into an oval about 25 × 15 cm on a floured sheet of baking paper.
Roll the two long sides in towards the centre to form thick raised rims, leaving a wide gap in the middle, then pinch the two ends together and twist them into points so the bread looks like a boat.

Fill each boat with the cheese mixture, keeping it off the rims, and brush the rims with a little milk. Slide the breads on their paper onto the hot trays and bake for 10–12 minutes, until the crust is golden and the cheese is bubbling.
Take them out, make a well in the cheese of each with a spoon and slip in an egg yolk. Return to the oven for 1–2 minutes, just to warm the yolk; it should stay runny.
Put a pat of butter on each and serve at once. At the table, stir the yolk and butter into the hot cheese and tear off pieces of crust to dip.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 6–8 minutes until hot throughout.
notes: For imeruli khachapuri, enclose the same cheese filling in a round of dough and bake or pan-fry it flat.

recipes.name: Khinkali (Georgian soup dumplings with beef and lamb)
recipes.description: Large pleated dumplings filled with peppery minced beef and lamb, onion and herbs, which turn into a pocket of hot broth as they boil. Eaten by hand: hold the knot, bite, sip the juices, then eat.

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt with the water and knead for 10 minutes into a stiff, smooth dough; khinkali dough is firmer than most so it can hold the juices. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, mix the meats, onion, garlic, coriander, caraway, chilli, pepper and salt in the bowl. Add the cold water a little at a time, squeezing and working the mixture with your hand for 3–4 minutes, until all the water is absorbed and the filling is loose and sloppy. This water becomes the broth inside.
Roll the dough out on a floured surface to about 2 mm thick and cut out 10 cm rounds (re-roll the scraps once). Roll the edges of each round a little thinner than the centre. You should get about 20.

Put a heaped tablespoon of filling in the centre of a round. Holding it in one hand, lift the edge with the other and fold it into small pleats, rotating as you go, making 15–20 pleats that gather above the filling. Pinch and twist the pleats together at the top to seal them into a knot, and set the dumpling on a floured tray. Repeat.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil and stir it gently. Lower in about 10 khinkali, stir once so they don't stick, and boil for 10–12 minutes from when they float, until the dough is tender and the filling is cooked through (71 °C).

Lift them out with the slotted spoon onto a platter, grind over plenty of black pepper and serve at once. To eat, pick one up by its knot, bite a small hole, sip the broth, then eat the rest, leaving the doughy knot on the plate.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked khinkali on a floured tray, then bag them; boil from frozen for 15 minutes. Cooked leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Pan-fry cooked khinkali in a little butter until golden and hot through.

recipes.name: Chakhokhbili (Georgian chicken and tomato stew with herbs)
recipes.description: Chicken braised with lots of onions and ripe tomatoes, garlic, blue fenugreek and coriander, finished with a big handful of fresh herbs. A homely Georgian stew to mop up with bread.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep frying pan with a lid

ingredients.name: Chicken thighs and drumsticks, bone-in and skinless
Blue fenugreek (utskho suneli), or ground fenugreek

steps.t: Peel the tomatoes: cut a small cross in the base of each, cover with boiling water for 30–60 seconds until the skin starts to curl, then drain and slip off the skins. Chop the flesh, keeping the juice.

Heat the heavy pot over medium-high heat and add the chicken in a single layer with no fat; let it sear and release its juices for 8–10 minutes, turning once, until golden in places. Add the butter and onions and cook for 10 minutes, stirring, until the onions are soft and golden.
Add the tomatoes and their juice, half the garlic, the chilli, ground coriander, fenugreek, paprika, bay leaf, salt and pepper. Stir well and bring to a simmer.

Cover and cook on low heat for 25–30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender, reaches 74 °C near the bone and the sauce has thickened. Uncover for the last few minutes if it is watery.
Stir in the chopped herbs and the remaining garlic and simmer for 2 minutes, then take off the heat and rest for 10 minutes so the herbs perfume the sauce.
Serve hot in deep plates with plenty of Georgian bread (shoti or tonis puri) or crusty bread, or with mchadi cornbread and a cucumber and tomato salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: The name comes from khokhobi, pheasant, the original bird; a whole chicken cut into pieces with its skin gives a richer sauce.

recipes.name: Lobio (Georgian spiced kidney beans with walnuts and coriander)
recipes.description: Red kidney beans cooked until creamy, then roughly mashed with fried onions, a garlic and walnut paste, blue fenugreek and lots of coriander. Served hot in clay pots with cornbread and pickles.

ingredients.name: Blue fenugreek (utskho suneli), or ground fenugreek

steps.t: Drain the soaked beans, put them in the saucepan with the bay leaf and cover with fresh water by 5 cm. Bring to the boil and boil hard for 10 minutes, skimming off the foam; red kidney beans must boil vigorously to destroy their natural toxins.

Lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 1–1½ hours, until the beans are very soft and creamy inside. Top up with boiling water as needed so they stay covered. Drain, keeping the cooking liquid.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onions for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.
Pound the walnuts, garlic, salt, ground coriander, fenugreek, savory and chilli in the mortar to a coarse, oily paste.

Return the beans to the pan and mash about half of them roughly with the potato masher, leaving the rest whole. Stir in the fried onions, the walnut paste and enough cooking liquid to make a thick, rustic stew. Simmer gently for 5–10 minutes, stirring, so the flavours combine.
Off the heat, stir in the coriander, parsley and vinegar. Taste for salt and sharpness.
Serve hot or warm, in clay bowls if you have them, with mchadi (cornbread) or bread, pickled vegetables and a plate of fresh herbs and radishes.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F); add fresh coriander before serving.
notes: With canned beans (3 cans, drained), skip the first two steps and mash them with a little water.

recipes.name: Kharcho (Georgian beef soup with walnuts, rice and sour plum)
recipes.description: A thick, warming beef soup with rice, soured with tkemali plum sauce and enriched with a paste of walnuts, garlic and Georgian spices, finished with a heap of coriander. Tangy, nutty and gently hot.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or food processor

ingredients.name: Blue fenugreek (utskho suneli), or ground fenugreek
Tkemali (sour plum sauce), or tamarind paste

steps.t: Put the beef in the stockpot with the cold water and bring to the boil, skimming off the foam for 5–10 minutes until the surface is clear. Add the bay leaves and peppercorns, cover and simmer gently for 1½ hours, until the beef is tender.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes until it darkens.
Add the onions and the rinsed rice to the broth and simmer for 15 minutes.
Pound the walnuts with 4 of the garlic cloves, the coriander, fenugreek, paprika, chilli and salt to a coarse paste (or pulse in a food processor). Loosen it with a ladle of hot broth.

Stir the walnut paste and the tkemali into the soup and simmer for 5–10 minutes, until the rice is tender and the soup has thickened slightly. Taste: it should be sour, nutty and gently spicy, so add more tkemali or salt as needed.
Take off the heat, stir in the remaining garlic (crushed) and the herbs, and rest for 5 minutes. Serve hot with Georgian bread or crusty bread.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F).
notes: Tkemali is a Georgian sauce of sour cherry plums, sold in bottles; tamarind paste or a little pomegranate molasses with lemon gives a similar sourness.

recipes.name: Ghapama (pumpkin stuffed with rice, dried fruit and honey)
recipes.description: A whole pumpkin filled with buttery rice, dried apricots, prunes, raisins, walnuts, honey and cinnamon, baked until the flesh is soft enough to cut in wedges. An Armenian New Year and Christmas centrepiece.

ingredients.name: Whole round pumpkin (about 3 kg)
ingredients.prep: lid cut off, seeds and fibres scraped out

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Wash the pumpkin and cut a lid around the stalk, about 12 cm across, angling the knife inwards so the lid sits back securely. Scrape out all the seeds and stringy fibres with a large spoon. Rub the inside with 1 tablespoon of the honey and the salt.
Bring a saucepan of salted water to the boil, add the rice and boil for 6–8 minutes, until half-cooked: soft outside but still firm in the middle. Drain well.
Mix the rice with the dried apricots, prunes, raisins, walnuts and cinnamon, then stir in most of the melted butter and 2 tablespoons of honey.
Spoon the filling into the pumpkin, filling it loosely to about 3 cm below the rim, as the rice swells. Drizzle over the water, the remaining butter and honey, and put the lid back on.

Set the pumpkin on the baking tray and bake for 1½–2 hours, depending on its size, until a skewer slides easily through the side of the pumpkin and the rice inside is tender. If the skin darkens too much, cover it loosely with foil.

Rest for 10 minutes, then carry it to the table whole. Cut it from top to bottom into wedges, so that everyone gets both soft pumpkin and fruity rice, and drizzle with a little more honey if you like.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat wedges, covered, in a 180 °C oven for 15–20 minutes until hot throughout.
notes: A dense, sweet pumpkin such as Crown Prince or kabocha works best; carving pumpkins are watery.

recipes.name: Shah plov (Azerbaijani crown pilaf in a lavash crust)
recipes.description: Saffron rice layered with lamb braised with dried apricots, raisins and prunes, sealed inside buttery lavash and baked into a golden dome, then turned out and cut like a crown. Azerbaijan's festive royal pilaf.
equipment: Deep heavy ovenproof pot or round tin (24 cm)

ingredients.name: Saffron threads
ingredients.prep: ground and steeped in 4 tbsp hot water

steps.t: Melt 2 tablespoons of butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat and brown the lamb in batches for 8–10 minutes. Add the onions and cook for 10 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper, add the water, cover and simmer for 1 hour, until the lamb is tender and the liquid has reduced to a little thick sauce. Stir in the dried fruit for the last 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring 3 litres of water with the 2 tablespoons of salt to the boil. Add the drained rice and boil for 6–7 minutes, until just al dente, then drain. Toss it gently with the saffron water and 3 tablespoons of the melted butter.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Brush the pot generously with butter. Cut the lavash into wide strips and line the pot with them, radiating from the centre of the base and overlapping, leaving about 10 cm hanging over the rim. Brush each layer with butter and make two layers in all.

Spread a third of the rice over the base and press it down lightly. Add half the lamb and fruit, then another third of the rice, the rest of the filling and the last of the rice. Fold the overhanging lavash over the top, patching any gaps with extra pieces, brush with butter and pour the remaining butter over.
Cover with a lid or foil and bake for 45 minutes, then uncover and bake for 15–20 minutes more, until the crust is deep golden and crisp; lift the edge with a knife to check the sides.

Rest for 10 minutes, then set a large platter over the pot and turn the plov out in one confident movement. Cut a circle in the top crust and lift it like a crown, or cut the whole dome into wedges at the table. Serve with a herb salad and pickles.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Roasted chestnuts are a classic addition to the filling. Some cooks make the crust from a simple dough (qazmaq) rolled thin instead of lavash.

recipes.name: Göyərti qutabı (Azerbaijani thin flatbreads filled with herbs)
recipes.description: Paper-thin half-moons of unleavened dough filled with spinach, coriander, dill and spring onion, cooked on a dry griddle and brushed with butter. Served warm with yogurt and sumac.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan, griddle or saj

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt, oil and warm water and knead for 8 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes so it rolls out paper-thin.

Mix the chopped spinach and herbs with the salt and squeeze them gently with your hands for a minute so they wilt and release their liquid; pour off the liquid. Stir in the spring onions, sumac and pepper.
Divide the dough into 12 balls. Roll each on a lightly floured surface into a very thin round, about 1 mm thick and 18–20 cm across.

Spread a thin layer of filling over one half of a round, fold the other half over and press the edges together, pushing out any air. Trim the edge with a small plate and a knife for a neat half-moon, or crimp it with your fingers.
Heat the dry frying pan or griddle over medium-high heat. Cook the qutab one or two at a time for 1–2 minutes per side, until the dough is cooked, dry and speckled with brown spots; don't add oil.
Brush each one with melted butter as it comes off the pan and stack them so they stay soft. Sprinkle with sumac and serve warm with yogurt for dipping.

recipes.storage: Best eaten warm; leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a dry frying pan for 1 minute per side.
notes: Meat qutab are filled with lamb mince, onion and pomegranate seeds; pumpkin qutab with squash cooked with onion and cinnamon.
